demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Ram Singh, an 80‑year‑old widower of Indian descent, retired from the U.S. Coast Guard after a 35‑year career of sea duty. In the early 1970s he was operating a rescue launch when a sudden collision with a fishing trawler—miscommunication of radio signals and a misjudged turn—caused a severe spinal injury to a young fisherman. Ram survived, but the guilt of having inflicted that pain left a scar that has endured for decades. The memory of the day was never a quiet recollection; it erupted in sudden, vivid sensory bursts whenever the world mirrored the scene: the wind‑tossed sea, the hiss of an alarm, the murmur of a conversation about plans for the future. Whenever Ram walks along the shoreline at dawn, the sight of waves matching the exact curve of the launch’s hull triggers a rush of dread, a sense that the danger he caused could recur. The mere sound of a siren on the radio—whether a fire alarm or a coast guard emergency call—instantly pulls him into that painful past, as if the air itself were a threat. Even talking with his grandchildren about the future makes him freeze, because the thought of a tomorrow he might lose mirrors the calamity he helped create. Each of these triggers forces his mind to swing toward the threat of another catastrophic event, and the same triggers pull up the fragmented, sensory‑rich memories he keeps locked away. The vividness of those memories, in turn, makes him feel defective, as if something irreparably wrong lies in his character. Ram’s self‑appraisals—he feels defective, hypervigilant, and blames his own character for the tragedy—have become the engine that drives his maladaptive coping. He tells himself, with a forceful conviction, that the accident “wasn’t really that bad,” a form of magical thinking that denies the true weight of his actions. He insists on positive reframing, telling himself that he saved the fisherman’s life in some small way, and tries to push every painful thought out of his mind through thought suppression. The belief that he is a flawed person feeds directly into these strategies; if he were a better sailor, he would not have caused the injury. The suppression he applies to the memory of the crash, however, only deepens the fragmentation, making the recollection harder to recall deliberately while keeping it alive in bursts of sensory reliving. These flashes reinforce his sense of threat, because each sudden, vivid image reminds him that the danger is still present. The more he tries to suppress the memory, the more it surfaces when the siren sounds, when the sea stirs, or when he speaks about the future. The threat that looms over Ram also spawns more maladaptive strategies. In an effort to feel secure, he always chooses the “safe” seat on a bus or in a meeting, the one closest to an exit or with a backrest, because he believes it will shield him from unexpected harm. Yet that very insistence on safety drives him to take unnecessary risks: he will volunteer for long maritime drills or operate the rescue launch in rougher weather than the weather forecast advises, convinced that proving his competence will absolve him of guilt. The threat of a repeat accident also forces him to avoid unfamiliar places—any new dock, new route, or unfamiliar town—so that he can assess danger in familiar terms. Each avoidance, in turn, triggers memories of the night the collision occurred, and the threat that memory holds. The cycle of threat, memory, and avoidance is self‑reinforcing; when Ram perceives a potential danger, the memory flares, the threat escalates, and he pulls back into a safe place, where the memory again is recalled, perpetuating the loop. The network of causes is wide. Each time Ram tries to reframe his thoughts positively, the underlying belief that he is defective becomes more entrenched, and that defectiveness feeds his avoidance. The avoidance, when triggered by sirens or unfamiliar settings, brings up the same memories again, which remind him of danger, which in turn strengthens the belief that he is a bad person. The same chain repeats whenever a piece of his past surfaces—whether in the smell of salt, the crackle of an alarm, or a conversation about the future—each trigger pulling him back into the memory, the threat, the appraisal, and the maladaptive strategy. Ram has now begun to feel the weight of the loop in his daily life. He cannot attend his grandchildren’s baseball games because a siren during a distant thunderstorm on the radio forces him to retreat to the kitchen. The anxiety of hearing a distant alarm has made him a recluse, avoiding the very coastal town he once loved. He has been unable to manage the finances of the small family home he shares with his sister, as each unfamiliar setting at the bank causes a surge of hypervigilance and the compulsion to sit in the most “secure” corner of the counter. The isolation, the constant threat, and the sense that he has failed himself drive him to the therapist’s office. He is most afraid that the next siren will bring the past back to life in full sensory detail, and he hopes to learn how to let those memories settle so he can move beyond living in constant fear.
